ILLEGAL ELECTRICAL CONNECTIONS (Durban)

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Dangerous webs of Illegal Electricity Connections threaten the economy, the electricity grid and claims lives. We investigate this deadly trend that’s sparked the need for service delivery and a se

Unique Selling Point:
- UNDERCOVER ELEMENT
- BRINGS IT HOME FOR OUR VIEWERS
- CONFRONT

Summary:
12 year-old Kyle O’Reilly was killed when he stepped on an illegal electricity connection while playing in the Umbilo Canal in Durban. He is not the first, and he won’t be the last to die because of illegal electricity connections.

Carte Blanche first covered illegal electricity connections in KZN in 2002. 18 years later, not much has changed. We call out eThekwini Municipality’s band-aid approach and ask what is being done to address the root problem.

Further information:
BACKGROUND
When most people think about illegal electricity connections, they think it is an informal settlement problem – it doesn’t concern South African that live in formal housing structures. That couldn’t be more wrong.

The death of Kyle O’Reilly brings this message home. Here is a kid that was killed while playing – a kid that was not living in an informal settlement. Every single day people are at risk in informal settlements – yet we don’t talk about it.

WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?
1. LOADSHEDDING: In the times of loadshedding – illegal electricity connections tap into an already overloaded system that is hobbling along in desperate need of maintenance – so it adds more pressure to an already crippled grid.
2. ECONOMY: illegal electricity connections take electricity for FREE – but nothing is for free – somewhere along the line – you and I are paying for it – be it through increased electricity costs or taxes.
3. DANGER: People are literally dying.

UNDERCOVER
No one has ever shown the process of “getting connected” in a community – we send in an operative armed with a hidden camera to meet with one of the guys offering this illegal service. We get the low down and then we can confront the guy.

INSIDER
We speak to community members who live in one of these settlements to get the inside track on the reality of their daily lives – the need for services and the fact they are left no option but to connect illegally – despite the danger.
THIS WILL BE A HIDDEN ID INTERVIEW FOR FEAR OF RETRIBUTION


SWEEP
The community of Seaview & Bellair are taking matters into their own hands and go in with local security companies and local police to disconnect illegal power wires. They have had enough – the municipality isn’t affective.

THE CHALLENGE
Taking the lines down don’t solve the problem – within a day – it’s all back up. So we plan to go in do – a sweep, and then come back the next day to see if the connections are back up (THEY WILL BE)

CONFRONT
We take on the Municipality in frank interview – 18 years later – same issues, no real solution – this simply isn’t good enough.

EXTRA COSTS

UNDERCOVER OPERATIVE IN DURBAN - R1500 per day - should be done in one day.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Electricity. It’s essential to everyday life, whether you live in a house in the suburbs or a shack in a township. People need it, and they’ll get it - even it means stealing it.

SIFISO: For now we don't have any option. // INT1 M4 // You can't live in it dark. No one can live in dark. INT2 M1//

VO: Impoverished communities around South Africa take matters into their own hands when municipalities fail to deliver basic services – but it’s doesn’t come without grave consequences.

LINK: Illegal electricity connections don’t just overload an already struggling electricity grid, it impacts on the economy in millions of Rands in lost revenue and it is dangerous – these make shift connections costs lives.

VO: 12 year-old Kyle O’Reilly was electrocuted while playing in the Umbilo Canal in Durban. His father, Wayne, is devasted.

WAYNE: // STUTTER STUTTER….. And it breaks my heart. I wont joke, it breaks my heart badly. I don't know that I've lost. I lost such a. Precious Gem. INT2 M1

VO: Kyle and his friends were playing along a nature trail on a Sunday afternoon. They were jumping over the sand banks when Kyle unwittingly touched a suspended cable. It was in fact, a live electrical wire.

WAYNE: When you grabbed a cable when had slipped That's when you started getting electrocuted and the kids went down to try and help him and assist him and they couldn't get close enough. INT3 M3

VO: Kyle died on the scene. It was illegal electricity connection that fed power to nearby informal settlement.

WAYNE: To see my son go out that way is that that is totally totally totally unjustified uncalled for. It's. It's wrong. By all means. Wrong wrong wrong. //INT4 M2

VO: But Kyle O’Reilly is not the first, and he won’t be the last to die because of illegal electricity connections. Fatalities are often under reported according to eThekwini Municipality.

It’s a daily reality for people like Sifiso Msomi who live in informal settlements all over South Africa.

SIFISO: Everyone knows this thing has only electricity and electricity is dangerous to us. INT1M8
MAC: How does this work. Is this where the sources is
SIFISO: We are getting the electricity wire from coming from the source. Then’s come here, from here and cannot be distributed to the houses INT4M1
MAC: But are you guys qualified?
SIFISO: No one is qualified, INT1 M10 What do it ourselves.

VO: Electricity Theft amounts to 4% of eThekwini Municipality annual losses, sitting at just over R300 million every year.

Across the country - it’s even become an income stream for some who take advantage of people who are desperate for basic services.

LINK: There are a couple of ways getting connected in an informal settlement – you can take your chances and do it yourself, alternatively someone in the community offers the service – either at a monthly connection fee ranging from R30 to R50 or you can pay once of fee of a couple of hundred bucks.

VO: In most informal settlements the illegal networks have already been established by amateur electricians known as Izinyokas – meaning Snakes. It’s a dangerous job, but the money is good – a once of connection could cost as much as R1500.

We sent in an operative to meet a guy who claims to know the ins and outs of illegal electricity networks.

CONNECTOR: it belongs to the municipal, but seeing that its there all you have to do is extend it towards the ground and then you hang the wire on top. cLIP 2
CONNECTOR: Connecting for your self is very dangerous because its very bad there. Clip 1

VO: HE claims he doesn’t do new illegal connections. He specialises in modifications to existing dodgy networks created by izinyokas.
CUT OUT UPSOUND FROM UNDERCOVER
His services are still illegal, but are quite a bit cheaper, because the risks are lower.

CONNECTOR: Its R600, it’s not negotiable. If I do it well, you can give me a bonus of a hundred Rands. CLIP 3

VO: We stopped him on the way to one of these jobs.

M7 MAC: Are you qualified
MAVA: No, I got to start afresh and do the trade test
MAC: you know what it’s illegal
M27 MAVA: I;m not a big mamba.

VO: The so-called big mambas or Izinyoka’s are hard to catch – because communities are reluctant to out these illegal connectors as they feel indebted to them for giving them electricity when municipalities fail them.

And if authorities manage to catch them, the current fining system is not a deterrent with fines as little as R500 - explains Sbonelo Mchunu from the Durban Metro Police.

MCHUNU: // if those people get caught either the community members or the illegal connectors // they pay that fine INT1 M6 // the fine does not fit the crime. /

VO: Technical Advisor for the KZN Electrical Contractors Association, Chris Collings, accompanied us to another informal settlement to check some of these connections.

MAC: Is this even an acceptable electrical work?
CHRIS: never never never. this is deadly. // This is not even. Two meters off the ground. // INT1 M2 end // when you touch that you create the current. // You need a hundred 200 milli amps. To kill you. And this will do it for you. INT1 M2 beginning

VO: Not surprisingly, the electrical work inside some of the structures were also not up to scratch.

CHRIS: Very hazardous and there's no protection. // This could cause a fire. // INT7 M1

VO: There are blatant hazards visible all over the settlement. Here, a piece of wood separates two cables that are creating an electrical short. To make matters worse, it’s near the communal tap.

CHRIS: // if you're standing in a pool of water and you touch the stick hanging down which is now a meter off the ground. It's another possible electrocution. INT3 M3

VO: The Durban Metro Police provide law enforcement support to eThekwini Municipality during official disconnection sweeps. Teams are physically threatened and the situation turns violent quickly explains Mchunu.

MCHUNU: // they get stoned //they get attacked at some point they had to shoot back using live ammunition to escape the attack from the community because their community just does not want. These disconnections to take place. INT1 M7

VO: But these disconnections are temporary explains Sifiso - communities jump into action as soon as the municipality leaves the settlements.

SIFISO: We try by all means to get another cable –
MAC: And you put it straight back
SIFISO: and. Try. To put it back. // cause there’s nothing you can do. INT2 M1

VO: While these communities are tapping in for free, Durban Ward Councillor Pete Graham says – nothing is for free, it comes at a cost to ratepayers and legal electricity users.

PETE: An electricity grid has to be balanced at all times so what we've got here is excess load being pulled out of the grid // if a cable has been put in here illegally it is has removed power from someone else so therefore it impacts everybody // INT1 M2

VO: Although these settlements are usually adjacent to suburban areas, they go widely unnoticed.

Mchunu believes the root problem with illegal connections is land invasions that lead to the formation of informal settlements.

MCHUNU: People move in illegally and they occupy that land.// INT1 M2 end // It becomes an establishment and then that establishment then must be followed by services the municipality is now supposed to provide. So the waste removal, water, electricity and so forth //INT1 M3

LINK: Even though Ethekwini Municipality had agreed to give us an interview, after countless calls, messages and emails – they refused to speak to us on-camera about illegal connections and pulled out at the last moment. CITY LINK

VO: In a subsequent email, the city stated it is “dedicated to controlling leaking revenue through theft by doing continuous sweeps and disconnections”. And spends over R100m every year on curbing electricity theft specifically.

Criticism though, is that the city is not doing enough to address illegal connections.

PETE: //The city is underresourced. Given the number of settlements like this and the number of illegal connections the city is behind the power curve all the time INT1 M4

VO: It’s a complex issue, of balancing the fight against criminality and providing essential services to communities observes Mchunu.

MCHUNU: As much as the city sends these units including metro police to go and get compliance // the city must also have another program. To electrify the area to connect properly to create an infrastructure that is legal in that informal settlement up until people have moved to the proper houses. INT1 M8

VO: But without a workable solution, it will remain a daily struggle for people like Sifiso – who are forced to steal electricity and risk their lives.

SIFISO: They are human beings like the others so they need everything
MAC: But are you willing to pay for it? INT1 M18
SIFISO: Yes, we are willing to pay for everything. // INT1 M18

VO: But ward councillor Graham feels the city is failing to address the needs of people.

PETE: // People don't want to move up to the middle of nowhere. They've got no access to resources. // where there's no employment, where there's no schooling where there's no police. And until the city realizes that it's them that is causing of this problem – politics hindering service delivery.


 
PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: Dangerous webs of Illegal Electricity Connections threaten the economy, the electricity grid and worst, kills people. We investigate this deadly trend that’s fuelled by ineffective service delivery.

PROMO 2
VO: Illegal electricity connections puts pressure on electricity grids, robs the economy of revenue and puts lives at risks with reckless networks running through informal settlements across South Africa.

PROMO 3
VO: The spotlight is cast on illegal electrical connections after a 12 year old boy was electrocuted in KZN. We investigate this deadly trend that threatens lives, the economy and electricity grids.

INSIDER We speak to community members who live in one of these settlements to get the inside track on the reality of their daily lives – the need for services and the fact they are left no option but to connect illegally – despite the danger. THIS WILL BE A HIDDEN ID INTERVIEW FOR FEAR OF RETRIBUTION SWEEP The community of Seaview & Bellair are taking matters into their own hands and go in with local security companies and local police to disconnect illegal power wires. They have had enough – the municipality isn’t affective. THE CHALLENGE Taking the lines down don’t solve the problem – within a day – it’s all back up. So we plan to go in do – a sweep, and then come back the next day to see if the connections are back up (THEY WILL BE) CONFRONT We take on the Municipality in frank interview – 18 years later – same issues, no real solution – this simply isn’t good enough.
